children: By Staff Writer

Kenya is opening its electronic cargo tracking market to private operators, ending the Kenya Revenue Authority’s exclusive control over tracking seals used to monitor goods moving under customs control to markets across East and Central Africa.

KRA has approved 15 private vendors to supply electronic tracking seals under a new multivendor system that will allow importers, exporters, transporters, clearing and forwarding agents, and bonded warehouse operators to choose their preferred provider.

The government-owned seals will be phased out by October 26, after which cargo under customs control will be monitored using devices supplied by the approved vendors.“The framework shall be based on private commercial agreement between the approved vendors and users,” KRA said in a September 11 public notice.

The change will affect cargo destined for regional markets that rely on Kenyan ports, Uganda, Rwanda, Burundi, South Sudan, eastern Democratic Republic of Congo, northern Tanzania, Ethiopia and Somalia.

Much of this cargo must be fitted with electronic tracking seals before leaving the port or other designated customs-controlled facilities, allowing KRA to monitor its movement along approved transit routes until it exits Kenya or reaches its destination.
The regional reach is particularly important for Uganda, which is the largest destination for transit cargo passing through Mombasa, followed by South Sudan, the DRC, Rwanda and Tanzania.

Mombasa handled a record 45.45 million tonnes of cargo in 2025, up from 40.99 million tonnes in 2024. Transit cargo increased 19.5 percent to 15.88 million tonnes, while container traffic rose 5.5 percent to 2.11 million TEUs.

The rising volumes have increased demand for customs services and cargo-monitoring equipment, particularly for transit trucks that must be cleared and fitted with tracking devices before leaving the port.
Shortages of KRA-owned seals have previously caused delays for transporters, adding to truck turnaround times and operating costs.

Shippers Council of Eastern Africa CEO Agayo Ogambi said allowing multiple suppliers could improve access to the equipment and reduce delays.“With continued increase for transit cargo now accounting for over 30 percent of the port throughput, 2,000 trucks on the road per day, the many vendors will possibly enhance competitiveness, reliability and efficiency,” Mr Ogambi said.
He said shortages of seals had contributed to delays and affected truck turnaround.

The new arrangement represents a major change from the government-controlled supply model used to monitor transit cargo and prevent goods destined for other countries from being diverted into the Kenyan market.

Under the Regional Electronic Cargo Tracking System (Rects), tracking devices transmit information to a central monitoring system, allowing customs authorities to follow cargo along designated routes.

The technology can detect tampering, unauthorised opening, excessive stoppages and deviations from approved routes. Electronic fuel seals used on petroleum tankers can also monitor fuel levels and detect sudden changes.
Rects links customs monitoring across East African Community systems and is an important component of regional transit controls.
For countries without direct access to the Indian Ocean, the system provides an additional layer of oversight as goods move from Mombasa through Kenya before crossing into neighbouring markets.
KRA will retain regulatory oversight even as it opens the supply market. Vendors must meet specified technical, operational, security and integration requirements before providing the devices.
The framework covers both dry cargo electronic seals and electronic fuel seals. The approved vendors will own and maintain the equipment and enter commercial agreements directly with users.

This will shift part of the operational responsibility from KRA to the private sector. Businesses will have to select suppliers, negotiate commercial arrangements and ensure their trucks and cargo-handling operations are compatible with the tracking system.

KRA has said users will be free to choose any of the 15 approved vendors. The list is available through the authority’s website, the Cargo Monitoring Unit at the Times Tower in Nairobi and Customs offices.
The opening of the market comes as cargo flows through the Northern Corridor continue to expand, making the reliability of tracking systems increasingly important to regional supply chains.

A delay in securing a tracking seal at Mombasa can hold up a truck carrying cargo destined for Kampala, Kigali, Juba, Bujumbura, eastern DRC or other inland markets. The resulting costs can extend beyond Kenya to importers, transporters, manufacturers and retailers in neighbouring countries.

For regional countries, which rely heavily on regional corridors to access seaborne imports, the speed and reliability of customs procedures at the Kenyan coast can affect the cost and predictability of their supply chains.
The Northern Corridor therefore links the performance of Kenya’s port and customs infrastructure directly to the competitiveness of businesses across the region.
The change also creates a new responsibility for KRA: ensuring that increased competition among suppliers does not compromise the integrity of the tracking network.

All vendors will have to maintain systems capable of communicating with Rects while meeting KRA’s cybersecurity and technical requirements. The authority will also need to monitor performance and compliance across a larger pool of service providers.

For businesses, the October 26 deadline leaves a short transition period. Importers, transporters, clearing agents and bonded warehouse operators will have to identify preferred suppliers and put in place the necessary commercial and technical arrangements.

The private-sector model could also create a new logistics service market around electronic tracking, with vendors responsible for supplying, maintaining and supporting the devices used by transport operators.
But the commercial arrangements will need to work without creating additional delays or costs that undermine the objective of improving cargo movement.
The transition comes as Mombasa handles record cargo volumes and the Northern Corridor serves increasingly important markets in East and Central Africa.
For logistics operators, the immediate concern will be whether the new system provides adequate availability of seals, technical support and reliable connectivity.
For KRA, the broader test will be whether the multi-vendor model can combine faster cargo movement with the customs controls required to protect transit trade and government revenue.
The change is therefore not simply a shift in who supplies electronic seals. It alters how an important part of the region’s cargo-monitoring infrastructure is provided and paid for.

For Kenya and its neighbours, reliable electronic cargo tracking has become part of the infrastructure determining how efficiently goods move from the Indian Ocean gateway to the region’s inland markets.
